title: How to work couching in cross-stitch
subtitle: Laying a thicker thread on the surface and catching it in place
excerpt: Couching is a surface technique used in cross-stitch to lay a thick thread or ribbon on the fabric and secure it with small catching stitches worked in single-strand floss. It adds a raised or textured line where a back-stitch would look too fine.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, couching chapter. William Morris-period embroidery treatises on surface stitching, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A surface technique where a thicker thread or cord is laid along the fabric and caught at intervals by small catching stitches worked in a finer thread underneath. Adds a raised, tactile line to a design.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: lays a heavier thread on the surface of the fabric and holds it in place with small vertical catching stitches. Where a

outline reads as flat and fine, a couched line raises above the fabric surface and draws the eye more strongly. Cross-stitch charts use it for borders, stems, and any outline that calls for visible weight or texture.
The laid thread and the catching thread are two separate lengths of

(or the laid thread can be a cord, ribbon, or metallic). The catching thread is typically one strand in a matching or contrasting colour. The laid thread passes through the fabric only at its start and end points; everything in between sits on top.

items.name: Laid thread
items.qty: One strand or more of floss, or a fine cord or metallic
items.substitutions: Any thread heavier than single-strand floss works

items.name: Catching thread
items.qty: One strand of floss in a matching or contrasting colour
items.substitutions: For an invisible catch, use the same colour as the laid thread

items.name: Two tapestry needles
items.substitutions: One needle per thread if you prefer to work them separately

content.text: Thread the laid thread in one needle and bring it up at the start of the line from below the fabric. Hold the thread along the path it will take across the surface.
Thread the catching thread in a second needle and bring it up just to one side of the laid thread, close to the start point.
Take the catching thread over the laid thread and back down just to the other side, forming a small vertical stitch that pins the laid thread flat. Pull gently, keeping the laid thread straight.
Space subsequent catching stitches evenly along the line, roughly every three to four Aida squares. Closer spacing for curves; wider spacing for straight runs.
At the end of the line, take the laid thread down through the fabric and end it on the back with the same knot or weave-under finish used for ordinary floss.

items.symptom: The laid thread is uneven, with loose sections between catching stitches
items.cause: Catching stitches spaced too far apart, or the laid thread was not held taut as each catching stitch was formed.
items.fix: Add more catching stitches, especially on curves. Hold the laid thread at the end of the line with a spare finger while working each catch.

items.symptom: The line curves or wanders from the intended path
items.cause: The laid thread was not guided along the chart line before each catching stitch was secured.
items.fix: Mark the intended path lightly on the fabric with a removable pen before starting. Place each catching stitch exactly on the marked line.

content.text: outlines on botanical pieces where the stem needs more presence than a single-strand back-stitch gives. Try it on any florals project that includes a thick main stem.
